newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Gvt spending may undermine Slovak economy - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gvt spending may undermine Slovak economy - analysts.

text.p: Differences between the Slovak government and the central bank over budget spending could reverse the favourable fiscal development recorded in the first quarter of this year, analysts warned on Wednesday.

"The NBS seems determined to continue its tight monetary policy of restricting mainly domestic lending activities, while the government has so far not revised its expansive investment programmes," Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB bank told Reuters.

The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) this week released data showing the country's average consumer price index (CPI) up 6.0 percent year-on-year in the first quarter just above the central bank's 5.7 percent forecast for the whole of 1997.
In addition, the central bank (NBS) said the development of the state budget in the first quarter had no adverse effect on key monetary criteria and was in line with monetary policy.

"The M2, CPI and budget may look good but the main budget-funded programmes, such as highway construction, will come later in the year and accelerate the M2 growth and boost inflation," said one foreign analyst.
The state budget showed a deficit of 3.45 billion crowns in the January-March period, up from a 361.0 million shortfall in the first two months of the year.

The key money supply measure, M2, rose 13 percent year-on-year in the first three months of 1997, down from a 20 percent increase in the same period last year. The NBS monetary programme plans M2 up 10.7 percent year-on-year this year.
But analysts said that despite favourable figures and what the NBS considers as good cooperation with the government on fiscal policy, differences still exist on further monetary development.

"On the one hand the central bank has called for the government to cut spending, while on the other the government is striving for greater influence in it. These two factors make good cooperation between the two just wishful thinking," the analyst said.

The government raised many analysts's eyebrows earlier this year with the appointment of former deputy finance minister Jozef Magula to the NBS governing board and the naming of Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik as a non-voting government representative at board meetings.

More disturbing, analysts say, is the 1997 budget -- forecast at a 36.9 crown deficit after a 25.5 crown shortfall in 1996 -- since it has multi-billion crown allocations for infrastructure projects, such as motorway construction of about 14 billion crowns, still to come from the state coffers.
The NBS says it will stick to its tight monetary policy to keep the currency stable and inflation under control.
So far, measures at the start of the year to limit domestic credit expansion have created a liquidity shortage pushing interbank money rates to record levels over 20 percent.
This, analysts said, is making it too expensive for local firms to refinance their activities through short-term credits -- a practice common even among large companies.

"In the end it may be local firms and the economy as such that will suffer from the interbank market situation as some firms may have problems tapping foreign financial sources and expensive domestic credits can endanger their existence," Kuklis said.
